sum: CATL is pursuing growth on several fronts at once, but the market is fixated on a simpler question: whether the battery giant can keep expanding volumes without surrendering pricing power. That tension was on display Friday, when the stock fell 3.7% after JPMorgan trimmed its targets, even as the company unveiled a far-reaching strategic partnership with aluminium producer Chinalco and moved a major lithium project closer to approval.
The dual-track story — ambitious capacity plans on one side, softer per-unit economics on the other — has given investors two very different sets of yardsticks to watch.

The US bank lowered its price target on CATL's A-shares to RMB300 from RMB310 on Friday, though it kept an overweight rating on that share class. For the H-shares, JPMorgan maintained a neutral stance. The common thread: passing on tax costs is proving harder than the brokerage had anticipated, and it also marked down its earnings-per-unit assumptions for the Chinese battery sector.

The downgrade landed alongside CATL's own third-quarter update, which showed profit growth decelerating. Net income for Q3 2026 rose 14.5% year on year to RMB21.2 billion, while revenue climbed 58.6% to RMB165.2 billion. According to Reuters, that was the weakest earnings growth in nearly two years, reflecting fiercer competition and cooling Chinese car sales.

Against that backdrop, Chairman Robin Zeng used an October 31 appearance to sketch out a far more expansive future. CATL expects to ship more than 1,000 GWh in 2026, he said, describing the company as entering the terawatt-hour era. For context, deliveries in 2025 totaled 661 GWh.

The overseas picture offers some support for that ambition. CATL's installations of electric-vehicle batteries outside China jumped 46.7% to 143.7 GWh between January and September 2026, according to SNE Research. That gave the company a 33.7% share of the segment.

Alongside the volume story, CATL is widening its grip on the inputs that feed those batteries. A strategic cooperation with Chinalco, disclosed in Ningde, covers research into new non-ferrous metal materials and the recycling of metals. It also takes in direct access to green electricity and support for global supply chains.

sum: CATL's battery installations outside China climbed 46.7% year on year between January and September 2026, according to data published Thursday by SNE Research. The figures, which track battery deployment rather than company revenue, also show the world's largest cellmaker lifting its share of that market from 28.6% to 33.7%, with overseas volumes reaching 143.7 GWh.

Yet the stock did not follow the volume story. On Friday, CATL shares shed 3.7% amid a sector-wide slump that media reports link to mounting difficulty in passing battery tax costs on to customers — a squeeze that has prompted JPMorgan to trim its earnings forecasts for Chinese battery makers.

Management is nonetheless projecting a steep delivery increase for the full year. Chairman and CEO Robin Zeng said on October 31 that CATL expects shipments of more than 1,000 GWh in 2026, up from 661 GWh in 2025 — a milestone he framed as the company's arrival in the terawatt-hour era.
Shareholders gave the plan their backing on November 2, approving financial support measures and the 2026 employee participation scheme at an extraordinary general meeting.

On the storage side, CATL and Octopus Energy, together with CATL subsidiary Ampace, signed a letter of intent on Tuesday to develop smart home-storage solutions, with European markets as the initial priority. Under the arrangement, Octopus Energy's software and customer platform would be paired with battery technology from CATL and Ampace. The document sets out a framework for joint exploration rather than a finalized product launch.

A second European initiative followed on October 27, when CATL and INTILION agreed to deploy CATL energy-storage systems totaling 3 GWh over five years. Germany, Switzerland and Austria rank among the target markets, alongside other territories. The two partners also intend to advance sodium-ion and lithium-ion battery technology in Europe.

CATL's storage push extends beyond the old continent. On October 28, the company unveiled its TENER+ battery storage system, rated at 9 MWh, in Melbourne, and announced letters of intent with Hitachi Energy, EPEC Group and UNSW Sydney covering project execution, grid connection and qualification.

sum: CATL shares closed Wednesday down 3.7%, caught in the wider selloff that swept technology stocks from Wall Street into Asian trading. But the day's headline number matters less than the test it frames: whether the battery giant can convert a growing stack of agreements and cleared permits into earnings that keep pace with its expansion.

Two fresh data points sit on either side of that ledger. JPMorgan trimmed its price target on CATL's A-shares to RMB 300 from RMB 310, keeping an "Overweight" rating, according to media reports. The bank's reasoning was pointed — the company faces a harder time passing battery-tax costs through to customers. The same day, a Hungarian court dismissed a lawsuit brought by local residents against CATL's Debrecen battery plant, removing a legal obstacle to the project.

The cost pass-through issue cuts to the heart of a tension running through the whole sector. Reuters reported a rally in Chinese clean-tech stocks after Democrats won control of Congress, with investors betting on stronger U.S. support for clean energy. CATL rode that wave. Political tailwinds can lift an entire industry, yet whether any single company benefits economically depends on its room to maneuver on pricing — precisely where JPMorgan's caution lands.

That makes the bank's stance a nuanced one rather than a reversal. The "Overweight" rating stays; only the target moves. For investors, the combination argues for a split-screen view: underlying confidence holds only as long as the cost burden stays manageable.

Beyond the cost question, project milestones keep arriving. On October 30, authorities in Yichun approved the environmental impact assessment for the Jianxiawo lithium mine project, operated by CATL subsidiary Yichun Times New Energy Mining. The same day brought the Debrecen court ruling. Both clear procedural hurdles; both gain economic weight only once they translate into operating progress.

The profit trend remains the sterner yardstick. Reuters reported on October 20 that CATL's third-quarter 2026 profit growth slowed to 14.5% — its weakest pace in nearly two years amid intensifying competition. Those results were described as the trigger for the subsequent share-price decline.

The distinction matters for anyone weighing the stock. A friendlier industry mood can lift a share price without altering a single company's business outlook. A plant coming online is a different kind of evidence — an execution step rather than an expectation. Even so, industrial progress and financial success are not the same thing, and the market would do well to keep them apart.

The rally gives CATL two separate measures to answer to. One points to possible political support; the other to expected profits. JPMorgan, for its part, trimmed its earnings estimates for the battery maker while keeping a positive rating on the shares. That combination — confidence paired with more cautious profit assumptions — is more instructive than an unqualified bullish call, because it holds optimism and lower forecasts side by side.

The tension is worth sitting with. Investors buying CATL on future earnings must factor in the reduced expectations. The positive verdict stands despite the downgraded projections, but its conviction ultimately rests on whether the company converts business opportunities into actual profit. Political expectations can move sentiment; an earnings-based valuation cares only about what the company delivers.

Global ESS Market Surges 73%; LG Energy Solution Races 355% in North America
sum: Global shipments of lithium-ion battery energy storage systems (ESS) reached 779.9 gigawatt-hours (GWh) in the first three quarters of this year, up 73% from 451.5 GWh in the same period last year, according to industry data. The third quarter alone came to 286.8 GWh, up 58% year over year and a new all-time quarterly high.

The standout takeaway from the figures, released on the 5th by market research firm SNE Research, is that the center of gravity for growth is shifting outside China. China remained the single largest market at 313.1 GWh, but shipments to the rest of the world totaled 466.8 GWh, or 59.9% of the global total — up from 57.3% in the first half. North America grew 71% to 122.3 GWh and Europe grew 87% to 131.2 GWh, driving the global expansion.

The scorecards of South Korea's two battery makers diverged sharply in North America. LG Energy Solution shipped 18.4 GWh in North America in the first three quarters, lifting its share there from 4.8% a year earlier to 15.0% — third place behind CATL (37.0%) and Hithium (16.5%). In the third quarter alone it shipped 8.1 GWh, overtaking Hithium (7.1 GWh) to take second place right behind CATL. North America accounted for 83% of the company's global shipments, and 96% of its North American volume was for power grids.

Samsung SDI shipped 7.1 GWh in North America over the same period, growing just 17%. Falling short of the overall market's growth pace, its share slipped from 8.6% to 5.8%. Still, its supplies for North American artificial intelligence (AI) data centers rose 68%, from 1.7 GWh to 2.8 GWh — a notable shift on the profitability front.

The two companies' combined North American share jumped from 13.4% to 20.9%. SNE Research said that as North America and Europe tighten tariffs and supply-chain regulations on Chinese-made batteries, demand for suppliers with local production capacity is translating into actual shipment volumes.

Globally, LG Energy Solution shipped 22.1 GWh, growing a whopping 355%, with its share more than doubling from 1.1% to 2.8%. Third-quarter shipments came to 10.1 GWh, up 51% from the previous quarter and marking its first time above the 10 GWh quarterly threshold. Samsung SDI grew 46% to 12.0 GWh, and posted 5.6 GWh in the third quarter, up 70% from the prior quarter.

sum: Gasgoo Munich- On October 29, IM Motors kicked off pre-sales for the LS8 NEO, the first full steer-by-wire, large five-seat flagship SUV under its NEXT·2028 strategy. Two trims—the 93 Max+ and 103 Max+—are available with a pre-sale price starting from 249,800 yuan. The official launch is set for November 5.

A standout moment of the event was the joint appearance of IM Motors and CATL. "The LS8 NEO comes standard across the lineup with CATL-customized, high-quality batteries," said Xu Yin, vice president of IM Motors. "By leveraging the quality assurance of two industry giants, we ensure consumers can buy with confidence."

Gao Huan, chief technology officer of CATL, noted: "In new energy vehicles, the battery is a focal point for both cost and safety. We and IM Motors share the philosophy that 'professional matters should be left to professionals,' allowing each side to leverage its strengths. With the LS8 NEO—whether in safety, low-temperature efficiency, or fast charging—we have achieved exceptional performance."

The LS8 NEO offers two battery options: a 93 kWh golden high-efficiency unit and a 103 kWh single-crystal ultra-energy unit, delivering CLTC ranges of 684 km and 752 km, respectively. Paired with SAIC's latest NEO electrification architecture and a full-domain 800V high-voltage platform, the vehicle can add 529 km of range in just 15 minutes. Even at a 20% state of charge, it can unleash over 370 kW of peak power, while energy consumption is as low as 15.2 kWh per 100 km under CLTC conditions.

Beyond the rigorous battery selection, the new model comes standard with a full steer-by-wire Digital Chassis. It features an ultra-small turning radius of 4.85 meters and rear-wheel steering of up to 24 degrees in both directions. It also features full-domain physical AI powered by Momenta's world model, along with flagship amenities like 4D mechanical massage seats, B&O premium audio, and an intelligent refrigerator. Essentially, the vehicle brings features typically found in luxury cars down to the 250,000-yuan pure-electric segment, offering a comprehensive leap in class.
Following the pre-sale conference, IM Motors Vice President Xu Yin, IM Motors CTO Xiang Jiao, and CATL CTO Gao Huan participated in a group media interview.

sum: Investing.com -- Australian lithium stocks fell on Monday, with smaller miners leading losses, as investors weighed a weaker outlook for battery demand and expectations of improving supply following a reduction in lithium price forecasts by Citigroup.

The declines followed a report by Bloomberg on Monday that Citi had lowered its lithium price forecasts for the next two years, citing slower battery demand growth, trade uncertainty and broader macroeconomic headwinds.

The bank cut its three-month lithium carbonate price target to $12,000 a tonne from $20,000, its hydroxide forecast to $12,000 from $17,000, and its spodumene forecast to $1,200 from $2,000, according to Bloomberg. It also reduced its estimates for all three materials through the end of 2028.
Citi warned that consumers could delay purchases and maintain lean inventories as supply improves in 2027 and uncertainty over demand remains elevated.
Sentiment and investor positioning are likely to remain dominant near-term price drivers, leaving risks skewed to the downside, Bloomberg reported, citing the bank's research note.

sum: CATL shares jumped 7.8% as a broad rebound swept through Hong Kong's technology, EV and industrial names following the previous session's sharp selloff. The advance snapped a run of seven consecutive losing trading days, according to media reports. What the rally does not do is settle the question investors actually care about: whether the battery giant can turn its aggressive build-out into profitable growth.

Reading the move as a verdict on CATL's business would be a stretch. A market-wide recovery speaks to appetite for equities in general, not to whether competitive pressure on the company has eased. No single company-specific catalyst has been identified as the driver of the full gain, and pinning the entire advance on one would overreach.

The distinction matters because CATL still faces fierce competition and pressure on profitability as it expands its battery-swapping operations. The reported rebound lifted several large stocks at once. For CATL, what counts is how the products and expansion plans it has announced actually land in the business.

On Tuesday the company unveiled its Tianxing II battery platform for heavy trucks, alongside plans for the Qiji battery-swap system. By CATL's own account, a truck battery can be exchanged in roughly five minutes.

The approach ties the battery offering to a build-out of swap infrastructure. That gives investors a more tangible operational theme than a general market bounce: CATL is not merely launching new products but widening the network that supports them. Reuters reported that the company plans 900 swap stations for heavy trucks in China by the end of 2026, with the network growing further through 2027. The next stage calls for 2,000 stations, and over the longer term CATL is targeting 10,000 locations. Those are goals, not figures already achieved.

A separate agreement adds another dimension. CATL and the BAIC Group have struck a strategic collaboration on battery swapping covering battery supplies, network expansion and a battery-bank model. Several BAIC brands are to be connected to CATL's Chocolate swap system, with an ecosystem targeted at a scale of one million vehicles. The pact links battery supply with infrastructure and a model for provisioning it, going beyond a standalone supply relationship.

sum: CATL still expects global demand for traction and storage batteries to grow 20–30% in 2027, a forecast the company reaffirmed in its own assessment of quarterly results published today. Yet the headline number that matters for investors sits elsewhere: sales are climbing far faster than earnings, and the gap between the two has become the central question hanging over the stock.

Shares fell 3.3% in the previous session as the market digested a profit miss that has forced a rethink of how the battery giant should be valued. The debate is no longer about whether CATL can keep growing revenue. It is about whether additional business can be converted into proportionally stronger profit.

The storage battery segment is expanding fastest. Shipments rose roughly 60% year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026, with storage accounting for about 25% of CATL's total battery volumes. That momentum underpins the company's confident demand outlook, though it leaves unanswered how profitably those extra volumes are being sold.

Industry forecasts point to a growing pie. BloombergNEF expects newly installed global energy storage capacity to rise 45% to 188 GW in 2026, driven by solar buildout, storage mandates and subsidy programs. Protectionism is simultaneously complicating market access for Chinese suppliers and shifting supply chains — a reminder that a larger global market does not automatically translate into unrestricted opportunities for CATL.

Third-quarter revenue climbed 58.58% year-on-year. Net profit, by contrast, advanced just 14.54% to RMB 21.2 billion — against analyst expectations of 41.2% earnings growth. CATL earned more than in the prior-year period but fell well short of forecasts.

The divergence is not a reported profit collapse. It is a question of why strong top-line growth failed to flow through to the bottom line. Management attributed the pressure to product mix, a consumption tax and a reduced export tax rebate. The benchmark Shanghai Composite Index fell 22.34 points, or 0.60%, to close at 3,713.03. The Shenzhen Component Index lost 0.82%, and the blue-chip CSI 300 Index was down 0.7% by the midday break.

The index opened at 3,740.57, briefly reached 3,743.08 and then drifted lower through the day. It touched a low of 3,703.12 in afternoon trading. Turnover on the Shanghai index was about 37.8 billion shares, below Tuesday's level, which suggests investors were reluctant to make big bets ahead of more third-quarter earnings.

The biggest drag was Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., the world's largest maker of electric vehicle batteries. Its shares fell 10% in both Shanghai-listed Shenzhen trading and Hong Kong after the company reported much slower profit growth for the third quarter. The company cited fierce competition and slower growth in Chinese auto sales.

Because CATL is one of the most heavily weighted stocks in mainland indexes, its drop pulled down the broader market and the new energy sector as a whole. Liquor makers were also among the worst performers. Big data and cloud computing companies held up better.

Market participants said investors were using consumer stocks to express doubts about China's domestic economy before more quarterly earnings arrive. Toymaker Pop Mart fell about 4% in Hong Kong trading by midday on expectations that its third-quarter results would disappoint, adding to the cautious mood.

The selloff came two days after data showed China's economy grew 4.5% in the third quarter from a year earlier. That was faster than forecast and a rebound from a three-year low in the previous quarter. Strong exports drove the gain while domestic demand stayed soft.

sum: In the late 19th century, the founders of Standard Oil, the predecessor of ExxonMobil, began buying shares of railway companies in their personal names. Jabez Bostwick, one of the founding partners, later simply served as the president of the New York and New England Railroad Company, while another partner Camden guarded the oil-producing regions for Standard Oil and financed the Ohio River Railway at the same time.

Over thirty years, these individual shareholdings quietly formed a network. In 1904, investigative journalist Ida Tarbell wrote the well-known assertion in The History of the Standard Oil Company: Standard Oil "holds shares in most of the large railway systems and has representatives on the boards of directors of almost all major railway systems".

At that time, Standard Oil under the management of John D. Rockefeller was the largest crude oil extraction, gasoline and lubricant production enterprise in the United States. For Standard Oil, taking shares in railways could not only ensure that it could obtain cheap and safe oil transportation routes, but also make railway companies themselves major customers for lubricant sales. It can be said that this method guaranteed Standard Oil's position in the industry to a certain extent.

On October 6, 2026, Bloomberg, citing people familiar with the matter, reported that DeepSeek's new round of financing is nearing completion, with a scale ranging from 800 billion yuan to 1 trillion yuan. Tencent and CATL have once again become one of the investors with the highest capital contribution. It has been only more than four months since CATL first appeared on DeepSeek's shareholder list.

As a leader in power batteries, CATL used to invest its capital in mining, materials and automobile companies: securing supply in the upstream and connecting customers in the downstream. Now, its investment tentacles are beginning to extend to large models, data centers, computing power operation, and embodied intelligence.
Why does a battery manufacturer invest in AI? The story of Standard Oil provides a perspective to understand CATL.
What CATL is looking for is not a new story unrelated to batteries, but the next batch of customers for batteries and electric energy, as well as new capabilities required to access these customers.

sum: European Lithium has spent most of this year riding the momentum of its pending takeover by Critical Metals Corp, but the deal now enters a phase where paperwork gives way to judicial scrutiny. The Supreme Court of Western Australia will hold its first hearing on the Scheme of Arrangement on September 15, a session that determines whether the merger's carefully mapped timetable holds or slips.

Under the proposed structure, Critical Metals Corp would absorb 100% of European Lithium's issued share capital along with all options listed on the ASX. Existing European Lithium shareholders would emerge with roughly 41% of the combined entity. Should the court green-light the scheme, separate meetings for shareholders and option holders are slated for mid-October, with completion targeted for early November — all contingent on both judicial and investor approval.

The shares closed yesterday at EUR 0.2150, down 2.9% on the day. That retreat has little to do with the merger itself, which by all available indications is proceeding on schedule without any negative developments. Instead, it reflects a broader malaise across lithium equities, triggered by softening raw material prices.

Lithium carbonate in China recently traded near a one-month low as rising output from Australian mines overshadowed supply concerns in the Chinese market. Mineral Resources has restarted its Bald Hill mine after an 18-month hiatus, and Core Lithium has likewise revived its Finniss project. Adding to the unease, CATL's Jianxiawo mine — which the company says accounts for roughly 4% of global lithium supply — continues to grapple with permitting hurdles after Chinese authorities revoked an environmental clearance.

That combination of rebounding supply and regulatory uncertainty at a major producer has made lithium stocks jittery across the board. Western producers including Albemarle and Chile's SQM have posted steeper declines than the broader Global X Lithium & Battery Tech ETF, according to media reports.

Zoom out, and the recent pullback looks more like a breather than a reversal. European Lithium shares remain up 137% year-to-date, a testament to the lift the Critical Metals takeover has provided over many months.

sum: China's battery giant pays suppliers in 265 days and collects from automakers in 54. That 211-day gap built a fortress of profit — and the automakers now funding its competitors are about to test how deep the moat really goes.

Two months earlier, the company reported first-half results: net profit attributable to shareholders of RMB 43.284 billion, up 41.98% year on year. Nearly RMB 240 million a day.
Profits are rising. The share price is falling. What the market is pricing now is how long CATL can keep earning at this rate.
CATL's days payable outstanding in the first quarter of 2026 was about 265 days. Its days sales outstanding was about 54 days.
Put those two numbers together. It takes CATL nearly nine months on average to pay upstream suppliers. Downstream automakers must pay CATL in less than two months. The gap is 211 days.

sum: China's CATL has solidified its dominant position in the global EV battery market outside China, surpassing a 34% share. Meanwhile, the combined market share of South Korea's three major battery makers—LG Energy Solution, SK On, and Samsung SDI—plunged more than 10 percentage points year over year to the 27% range. The sharp contraction in the North American EV market dealt a direct blow to the Korean companies.

According to data compiled by SNE Research, a South Korea-based energy market research firm, total battery deployment in EVs, plug-in hybrids (PHEVs), and hybrids (HEVs) registered outside China from January through July this year reached approximately 316.2 GWh. That represents a 25.8% increase from the same period last year, outpacing the 20.4% growth rate of the overall global market during the same period. With China's domestic market showing signs of saturation, markets outside China effectively drove overall growth.

However, even as the market expanded, deployment by South Korean manufacturers actually declined. The trio's combined deployment fell 8.9% year over year to 86.1 GWh. As a result, their combined market share dropped 10.4 percentage points from 37.6% in the same period last year to 27.2% this year.

Breaking down by company, LG Energy Solution maintained its No. 2 position in the non-China market with 51.6 GWh, but deployment slipped 1.7% and its share fell 4.6 percentage points from 20.9% to 16.3%. SK On posted 22.2 GWh, down 9.9%, with its share declining from 9.8% to 7.0%. Samsung SDI recorded 12.3 GWh, a steep 29.4% drop—the largest decline among the top 10 players—and its share contracted 3.0 percentage points from 6.9% to 3.9%.

The underperformance of the three Korean companies effectively stemmed from the North American market. Their combined North American deployment plummeted 42.9% from 38.8 GWh in the same period last year to 22.2 GWh this year. In contrast, deployment in Europe rose from 44.4 GWh to 47.4 GWh, and in Asia from 9.5 GWh to 13.2 GWh. Analysts point to EV sales adjustments by North American customers, generational transitions of certain models, and production plan cutbacks as factors blocking volume recovery.

During the power battery industry's boom years, CATL prioritized heavy investment in capacity expansion and cutting-edge R&D, keeping dividends relatively restrained. Now, the implementation of a sizable interim payout suggests the company is starting to balance operational focus with long-term shareholder returns.

On the fundamentals, steady cash flow is what makes this payout possible. As a top global supplier of power batteries, CATL commands a dominant share of the automotive market. At the same time, its energy storage business is expanding rapidly, emerging as a vital second growth engine. Together, these two pillars build a solid foundation for operating cash flow, creating the conditions for consistent shareholder rewards.

sum: First Batch Order Marks China Battery Exchange's Entry into Commercial Deployment Under CATL Partnership

Jinhua, China, July 20, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Kandi Technologies Group, Inc. ("Kandi" or the "Company") (NASDAQ GS: KNDI), a global innovator in intelligent equipment and a technology-driven platform company, today announced that its wholly-owned subsidiary, China Battery Exchange (Zhejiang) Technology Co., Ltd. ("China Battery Exchange"), has secured an equipment procurement order from QIJI Energy (as defined below), the heavy-truck battery swap brand under Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited ("CATL"). Pursuant to the order agreement, China Battery Exchange will provide end-to-end services across eighteen heavy-truck battery swap stations, encompassing equipment manufacturing, delivery, site deployment, and after-sales maintenance.

China Battery Exchange secured its first heavy-truck battery swap station equipment order from CATL in August 2025 under a Framework Procurement Agreement. Building on that foundation, China Battery Exchange entered into a three-year strategic cooperation agreement in January 2026 with Times QIJI Green Energy Technology (Shenzhen) Co., Ltd. sum: Lithium carbonate futures in China fell ~10% over two trading sessions, dropping to a 10-week low of approximately 157,000 yuan ($23,175) per tonne on Tuesday following market speculation that China's EV battery giant, Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. (CATL), may soon restart its massive Jianxiawo mine.

Reports from authorities in Jiangxi Province show that CATL's Jianxiawo lithium mine in Yichun passed a preliminary land pre-review and site selection, with the Jiangxi Provincial Department of Natural Resources issuing a "Project Land Use Pre-Approval and Site Selection Opinion", valid from June 17, 2026, through June 17, 2029.

The approval report has also extended losses for lithium miners, with Lithium Americas (NYSE:LAC) cratering 15.2% over the past 30 days; Sigma Lithium Corp. (NASDAQ:SGML) has lost 14.8%, Atlas Lithium Corp. (NASDAQ:ATLX) has declined 10.2%, Albemarle Corp. (NYSE:ALB) is down 14.8% while Sociedad Química y Minera de Chile S.A. (NYSE:SQM) has shed 5.6% over the timeframe.

Located in Jiangxi Province, China, the Jianxiawo mine is one of the largest hard-rock, lepidolite-hosted lithium deposits in the world. Lepidolite is a lithium-bearing mica mineral comparable to the more common spodumene, which is composed of lithium and aluminum silicate. While it yields less lithium per ton of raw ore compared to spodumene, the sheer scale of the Jianxiawo lithium deposits makes it a force to reckon with, with the mine capable of producing ~46,000 tons of lithium carbonate annually, roughly equivalent to 3% of the global lithium supply.

The pullback is a reversal from the early-year rally when lithium carbonate futures spiked past 200,000 yuan per tonne driven by supply disruptions as well as an unexpected surge in demand from the grid-scale energy storage sector.

Global supply of lithium carbonate took a hit after major mining operations, including the Jianxiawo mine, faced extended shutdowns and permit delays. Back in February, Zimbabwe's government suspended the export of 14 critical metals, including lithium concentrates, indefinitely in a bid to curb leakages and force foreign operators (largely Chinese) to build local processing plants.

Sodium-Ion Batteries Poised for Breakthrough: 37% Market Share, $800 Billion Investment by 2035
sum: Sodium-ion batteries are rapidly emerging as the next-generation low-cost alternative to lithium-based energy storage. Global investment bank Morgan Stanley forecasts that sodium-ion batteries will capture 37% of the total battery market by 2035, with related investments reaching $800 billion (approximately ₩1,229 trillion).

According to a Morgan Stanley report cited by the Financial Times on June 23, sodium-ion battery market share is expected to jump from roughly 2% in 2027 to 20% by 2030, before expanding to 37% in 2035. The report identifies cost competitiveness as the primary growth driver, analyzing that sodium-ion batteries could become 30-40% cheaper than the currently dominant lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries.

The key to cost reduction lies in material composition. Sodium-ion batteries can significantly reduce the use of expensive lithium, copper, and graphite, while allowing aluminum to replace copper in current collectors, thereby lowering raw material costs. Additionally, sodium is widely distributed throughout the Earth's crust, meaning supply chain dependence on specific countries is far lower than for lithium and cobalt—a significant advantage in terms of geopolitical risk.

Low-temperature performance is another differentiating factor. Sodium-ion batteries maintain relatively stable electrolyte flow even in extreme cold conditions. While LFP batteries can lose roughly half their capacity at ultra-low temperatures, sodium-ion batteries are known to retain over 90% of their capacity.

China is moving fastest on commercialization. CATL (300750.SZ) and BYD (002594.SZ) are already pursuing mass production and vehicle integration of sodium-ion batteries. In April, CATL signed a contract to supply 60 GWh of sodium-ion batteries over three years to Beijing HyperStrong Technology. China's central government has also directed power companies to expand the use of sodium-ion batteries in energy storage power plants by 2027.

CATL has gone a step further. After unveiling its LFP-based Tener Stack ESS in Munich last year, the company recently debuted the Tener sodium-ion ESS at the same venue, featuring a design life exceeding 25 years.

items.t: CATL, The World’s Largest Battery Maker, Is Almost As Profitable As Toyota
sum: For decades, the automotive industry's biggest profits flowed to the companies designing, building, and selling vehicles. Today, that balance is shifting rapidly as electrification transforms the industry's value chain.

A striking example emerged from China this quarter. Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited, better known as CATL, posted first-quarter profits so large that the world's biggest battery manufacturer nearly matched the earnings of Toyota, the world's largest automaker.

Even more remarkably, CATL generated more profit during the first three months of 2026 than seven major Chinese automakers combined, highlighting just how much influence battery suppliers now wield in the global EV market.
The numbers underscore a growing reality: in the electric era, the companies supplying batteries may become just as powerful as the brands building the vehicles themselves.
CATL reported first-quarter 2026 revenue of 129.13 billion yuan ($17.9 billion), alongside net profit attributable to shareholders of 20.7 billion yuan ($3.06 billion).
Those figures are impressive on their own, but the comparison with China's largest vehicle manufacturers tells the bigger story.

According to industry data, CATL's quarterly profit exceeded the combined earnings of seven major Chinese automakers, including BYD, Geely, Chery, SAIC, Great Wall Motor, Seres, and Changan. sum: Autoblog and Yahoo may earn commission from links in this article.

There's a quiet but seismic shift happening at the top of the automotive food chain, and it doesn't involve a single car being sold. CATL, the China-based company that makes the batteries going into most of the world's EVs, posted a net profit of around $3 billion in the first quarter of 2026. That alone would be impressive. What makes it remarkable is who it leaves in the dust. CATL's profit exceeded the combined earnings of seven major Chinese automakers, according to CarNewsChina. Essentially, we have a supplier out-earning its entire customer base in one quarter.

Here's the thing about that combined figure from seven of China's biggest car companies: it still fell short of CATL's $3 billion by nearly half a billion dollars. None of those automakers individually crossed even a quarter of CATL's profit. The battery giant also held nearly half of China's EV battery market in Q1, growing its share year-on-year despite a slowdown caused by the phasing out of government subsidies.

Toyota, which sells roughly 10 million cars a year, reported results for the exact same January-to-March period. Operating profit came in at around $3.8 billion, just enough to edge past CATL, but only just. Further, that number is only after a punishing 49 percent year-on-year collapse driven by US tariffs and rising Chinese competition. A year earlier, Toyota's quarterly net income was $5.8 billion. This quarter, a company that makes no cars at all came within striking distance of matching it. The world's biggest automaker is still ahead. But a battery supplier breathing down its neck is not a headline Toyota would have written for itself.

sum: According to data from the China Passenger Car Association, CATL achieved a market share of 50.1% in the electric vehicle battery sector in the first quarter of 2026. This figure represents CATL’s estimated production share in the domestic market. It is an estimate, as the first quarter has not yet concluded—five days remain in March.

Regardless, the portal Car News China reports that CATL has regained this level of dominance in China for the first time in five years. In 2021, the company already held half of the domestic market, which at the time had a significantly smaller total volume. Incidentally, China’s total production volume of EV batteries for the first two months of the year reached 310 GWh, representing a 22% increase compared to the previous year.
But Car News China emphasises: “However, the proportion between produced and installed packs reached the historical low of 19%.” Currently, a significant volume is being produced for stock.

What stands out is CATL’s strategic positioning: the company dominates the ternary NMC battery segment in China while simultaneously expanding its presence in the LFP segment. The figures reflect this: CATL’s market share for NMC batteries reached 81.6% between January and March. Its market share for LFP batteries stood at 41% in the first quarter—’the highest [level] in four years,’ according to Car News China.

As the table shows, CATL leads by a significant margin. The second-largest domestic battery manufacturer in the first quarter was BYD, with a 17.5% market share, representing a 4.3% decline compared to the previous year. Car News China describes this as BYD’s ‘weakest result in five years.’ However, the company, which operates solely in the LFP segment, holds a 22.6% share of the LFP battery market. In this segment, the gap to CATL is not as pronounced.

Overall, it is clear that most manufacturers focus on either NMC or LFP battery chemistries. Only CATL and CALB pursue a dual strategy, while other manufacturers largely concentrate on a single chemistry—more frequently LFP than NMC. Consequently, the LFP market is more competitive, whereas CATL has pulled far ahead in the NMC battery segment with the aforementioned 81% market share. Only SVOLT and CALB still hold market shares above 5%.

sum: JPMorgan Chase's (JPM) latest research report indicates that despite BYD (01211.HK) launching a significantly upgraded second-generation fast-charging battery (Blade Battery 2.0), the expected negative impact on the global power battery leader Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL) (300750.SZ / 03750.HK) is limited. The firm simultaneously raised its target price for CATL's H-shares from HK$640 to HK$650.

The report suggests that as both BYD and CATL accelerate their deployment of ultra-fast charging technology, market focus on the competition between the two giants remains high. However, JPMorgan's analysis points out that the launch of BYD's new battery technology poses a direct competitive pressure on CATL that is within a manageable range. Conversely, the industry-wide transition trend towards ultra-fast charging may bring positive spillover effects to the supply chain, creating new growth avenues.

Regarding specific market expectations, JPMorgan anticipates that BYD will leverage its technological iteration to expand its market share in overseas automotive sales from a relatively low base. However, in the more fiercely competitive domestic Chinese market, BYD's share may face moderate erosion.

Despite raising the H-share target price, JPMorgan downgraded its rating on CATL's H-shares from "Overweight" to "Neutral" based purely on valuation considerations. The report explains this adjustment is primarily because CATL's H-shares currently trade at a premium of over 40% compared to its A-shares, making their valuation relatively less attractive.

Notably, JPMorgan maintains its "Overweight" rating on CATL's A-shares and on BYD. The firm explicitly stated that CATL's A-shares remain its preferred investment target in China's battery sector. This reflects the firm's continued positive outlook on CATL's long-term fundamentals and industry-leading position.

This rating adjustment highlights how international investment banks distinguish between the different valuation logics of the A-share and H-share markets when analyzing leading Chinese companies. For companies listed in both mainland China and Hong Kong, share price differentials often become a key factor influencing ratings.

sum: Shanghai Jiao Tong University has received the largest single donation in its 130‑year history, a landmark stock gift from the controlling shareholder of Chinese battery giant Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., Limited, better known as CATL. The donation comes just days before the university launches a series of events to mark its 130th anniversary and underscores the deepening ties between China’s most powerful technology industrialists and the country’s elite research universities.
The gift, announced in Shanghai, will be made not by CATL directly but through Xiamen Ruiting Investment Co., Ltd., the investment vehicle that holds the largest stake in CATL.

Xiamen Ruiting plans to transfer 5 million CATL shares to the Shanghai Jiao Tong University Education Development Foundation, to be used in support of the university’s long‑term educational development. At recent trading prices, the shares are valued at about $291 million dollars, setting a new record for philanthropy to the institution.

Behind the structure and corporate names is a single, pivotal figure: Zeng Yuqun, also known internationally as Robin Zeng. Born in Ningde, a coastal city in Fujian province, Zeng studied at Shanghai Jiao Tong University as an undergraduate before going on to found CATL, which has since become the world’s dominant manufacturer of lithium‑ion batteries for electric vehicles.
He is the founder, chairman and chief executive of CATL, and he is also the ultimate owner and actual controller of Xiamen Ruiting, the entity now making the donation on his behalf.

Regulatory filings and market research have long identified Xiamen Ruiting as Zeng’s personal investment and holding company, through which he controls a stake of just over one‑fifth of CATL’s equity and exercises effective control over the listed group. The 5 million shares earmarked for Shanghai Jiao Tong University represent only a small fraction of that position, but they carry enormous symbolic weight: they mark a deliberate transfer of personal wealth, in the form of core equity in one of China’s flagship industrial champions, into the endowment of a university that helped shape Zeng’s early career.

items.t: SNE Research: CATL continues to dominate global battery market
sum: Last year, the South Korean market research firm SNE Research recorded a total production volume of 1,187 GWh of battery cells for electric vehicles, marking the first time the 1,000 GWh threshold was surpassed. This represents a 31.7% increase compared to the 901.4 GWh produced in 2024.

By far the largest manufacturer of electric vehicle batteries remains the Chinese company CATL. The Ningde-based firm increased its production from 342.5 GWh to 464.7 GWh, achieving a growth rate of 35.7%, outpacing the overall market. According to SNE’s analysis, CATL grew its market share from 38.0% in 2024 to 39.2% in 2025. This growth was partly driven by a particularly strong December; for the period between January and November 2025, SNE Research recorded a market share of 38.2%.

CATL is thus the only battery provider with a market share exceeding 30%—and even 20%. In second place, BYD is listed by SNE Research with an annual production of 194.8 GWh. While this represents a 27.7% increase compared to the 152.6 GWh produced in 2024, BYD’s growth was slower than the overall market, causing its market share to dip slightly from 16.9% to 16.4% in 2025. Nevertheless, CATL and BYD, as the largest Chinese manufacturers, together account for 55% of the market; more than half.

Notably, in the evaluation from January to August 2025, SNE Research had still recorded BYD with an 18.0% market share, and over 50% growth. After just eight months, BYD had already reached 124.8 GWh. However, growth appears to have slowed significantly in the last four months of the year.

All other manufacturers now hold only single-digit market shares, marking a shift from 2024, when LG Energy Solution still accounted for 10.9% of EV battery production. Although the South Korean manufacturer increased its production by 11.3% to 108.8 GWh last year, it fell to a 9.2% market share due to the faster growth of competitors, though LGES still maintains a comfortable lead in third place.

Following CATL and BYD are CALB from China, with 62.6 GWh (5.3% market share), Gotion High-Tech (4.5%), and SK On from South Korea (3.7% of global production). Japan’s Panasonic holds the same market share as SK On. Rounding out the top ten are Eve Energy (2.6%), Samsung SDI (2.4%), and Svolt Energy (2.4%).

'They're just so much further ahead': How China won the world's EV battery race
sum: In 2005, China only had two EV battery manufacturers. Twenty years later, it produces more than three-quarters of the world's lithium-ion cells. How did it happen?

At the 2008 Beijing Olympics, athletes, journalists and officials from all over the world were transported by a fleet of sleek buses sporting a white, blue and green design as they zipped between different venues in the Chinese capital.

Different from the diesel-powered vehicles that ruled Beijing's streets at the time, the Olympic buses, numbering around 50, ran on lithium-ion batteries to help Beijing host a "green and high-tech" Olympic Games. It also marked the country's first foray into creating a lithium-ion battery industry for electric vehicles (EVs), laying the groundwork for China's ascension to world leader of this technology two decades later.

The Olympic e-bus campaign had been set in motion as soon as Beijing won the bid in 2001, according to a 2020 documentary aired by China's state media. But developing and producing EV batteries for the global event was no easy feat.

In late 2003, Mo Ke and his colleagues at the Beijing New Materials Development Centre – a government-affiliated research institute – were tasked to analyse China's lithium battery industry as part of Beijing's preparatory work for the Olympics.

But back then, China's lithium battery industry was "very small" with only two EV battery producers, as Mo's team found. In 2005, they hosted China's first conference for the lithium battery industry as a part of their research.
"All companies in the industry came, but there were only around 200 people in total," Mo says.

items.t: LFP Cells Set To Dominate the EV Market As CATL Announces Massive Improvements
sum: Two dominant chemistries are dueling for supremacy in the Li-ion battery industry: lithium iron phosphate (LFP) and nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC). Both have their strength and weaknesses, with NMC cells offering higher energy density and power capabilities, and LFP cells excelling in durability and safety. Similarly, NMC cells are less stable and have shorter life cycles, whereas LFP cells have a lower energy density and have reduced performance in low temperatures.

These characteristics have favored NMC cells for high-performance applications like premium EVs, while LFP cells have been mostly used in low-cost EVs and stationary battery energy storage systems (BESS). However, in the past years, the differences have been blurrier, mostly thanks to advancements in LFP cells. Modern LFP cells have almost closed the gap with NMC in terms of energy density, while retaining their main advantages: durability and safety.

These advancements were obvious for a long time, with industry analysts predicting in 2022 that LFP market share will surpass nickel-based chemistries by 2028. About three years later, LFP batteries already account for over 80% of the Chinese market, recording a 42.5% increase YoY in January through September 2025 installations. Worldwide, LFP cells are projected to account for 60% of the Li-ion battery market at the end of 2025.

CATL, the biggest battery manufacturer in the world by far, has been a big supporter of LFP cells. The Chinese company has developed the most advanced LFP cells, with its current fourth-generation LFP cells surpassing the industry's mainstream products in energy density, lifespan, and power output. However, CATL has already started mass production of its fifth-generation of LFP cells with improved characteristics.

The announcement was made during the 2025 World Power Battery Conference held in Sichuan (China). Robin Zeng, CATL's founder and CEO, said that the new cells achieved "new breakthroughs in energy density and cycle life," without providing more details. Zeng also provided updates on new battery technologies under development. These include R&D efforts for solid-state batteries, which CATL hopes to reach small-scale production by 2027.
